pageCache.text:

Nurturing Values
Focusing on wellbeing and relationships and sustainability
Enquiring
Listening carefully to others, learning together for the benefit of all
Purposeful Learning
Always working hard, trying your best and developing a growth mindset and metacognition​
Sustainability
Enjoying and appreciating the simple things. Behaving in a loving and caring way
The children say...
Our school is a calm, friendly and enjoyable place to be
Music at NEPS
A very warm welcome to North Ealing Primary School – a vibrant, popular and inclusive three-form entry primary school serving Pitshanger and the surrounding areas.
There is a real buzz about life at North Ealing. Our children are enthusiastic, curious and proud of their school, and staff know and care greatly about the children that they teach. Despite being a large school, we have a wonderfully warm family feel, where children are nurtured, valued and supported to flourish.
We give every child the best possible start. Excellent teaching, an ambitious and engaging curriculum and a wealth of memorable, exciting and meaningful experiences both in and out of the classroom enable our children to develop confidence, discover their talents, and most importantly, develop a genuine love of learning.
We have high expectations for every child, supporting them all to make excellent progress and be the best that they can be. Kindness and mutual respect are key, and we are very proud to celebrate the cultures, backgrounds and diversity that make our community so special.
Our specialist PE, Music and Spanish teaching brings additional expertise and excitement to the well-planned and engaging curriculum. We are also a Platinum Voice 21 School, placing Oracy at the heart of learning and providing all of our children with the skills and confidence to express themselves freely, listen to others and use their voice constructively. Learning and development continue beyond the classroom too.
Through OPAL (Outdoor Play and Learning), our playgrounds are vibrant, creative spaces where children explore, play, collaborate, take appropriate risks and have fun.
Our four core principles of: Nurturing values, Enquiry, Purposeful learning and Sustainability run through everything we do. They can be seen in our classrooms, curriculum, our playgrounds and in the way our children, learn, play and care for one another.
Parents and carers are a hugely important part of North Ealing. We work closely with families and welcome parents into school at every opportunity – to share learning, celebrate achievements, enjoy performances and events. This partnership between children, staff and families creates a strong sense of community and belonging that makes North Ealing so special.
We fully understand the needs of busy family life and ensure our extended-day provision (Breakfast Club and After School Club) is easily accessible to all that need it, giving families convenient wraparound care within their school community.
Whether you are already part of our North Ealing family, are joining us for the first time or considering the school for your child, I hope our website gives you a flavour of what makes our school such a happy and exciting place.
As Head teacher, I am incredibly proud to be part of this community. If you are considering North Ealing for your child, come and see us in action.
Meet our children and staff, see the learning and play taking place and experience the warmth, energy and unmistakable buzz of North Ealing for yourself.
Mrs H. Holton | Headteacher

Mission, Vision and Ethos Statement
Mission (Our purpose)
Our purpose at North Ealing Primary is to inspire learners who are happy, confident and courageous by working inclusively with our families, promoting equality and fostering a strong sense of belonging within our diverse community.
Vision (What we deliver)
At North Ealing Primary we inspire and nurture all our children to become aspirational, lifelong learners through an inclusive, ambitious and engaging curriculum.
Ethos (How we do it)
At North Ealing Primary School, our Learning Values and curriculum principles shape every part of school life. Guided by British Values and the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child, we realise our vision to create an inclusive environment where every pupil is valued, heard and ready for the next stage of their education.
We work together to provide the best teaching and learning environment for children, families and staff, shaped by our Learning Values, Behaviours for Learning and Curriculum Principles:
Our School Mission, Vision and Ethos Statement

NEPS Learning Values
Our Learning Values and Behaviours for Learning
C - Creative
H - Harmonious
I - Independent
L - Lifelong Learners
D - Determined
R - Respectful
E - Engaged
N - Nutured
Our 4 Core principles underpin the organisation of our curriculum:
1. Nurturing Values.
Underpinned by our Learning Values, we develop every child so that they can experience life to the fullest and are ready for the next stage of their education
2. Enquiring.
With big questions, big ideas and an investigative nature, we allow children to generate their own questions, think critically, forge and develop meaningful connections of the key concepts
3. Purposeful Learning.
We have an understanding of concepts we want children to know at the end of each year. And we believe in making all learning purposeful by making links, providing context and relevant enrichment
4. Sustainability.
A considered way of life – caring for the environment and each other is embedded across our curriculum with real-life implications being taught in many areas of the curriculum and addressed via SMSC, British Values and teaching of Unicef Rights
British Values at North Ealing Primary School
At North Ealing, we are developing our curriculum and in particular our Spiritual, Moral, Social and Cultural programme in order to incorporate ‘British Values’. Alongside our school learning values we reinforce these values regularly in the following ways:

NEPS Personal Development and Wellbeing
Personal Development and Wellbeing at NEPS
At North Ealing Primary School, we believe education is about far more than academic achievement. We are committed to nurturing happy, confident and aspirational pupils who are equipped to thrive both now and in the future. As a Rights Respecting School, we place children’s rights at the heart of our ethos and daily practice – we ensure that every pupil understands their rights. Our approach to personal development focuses on character, values and a strong sense of responsibility and citizenship. Through the PSHE and RHE curriculum, pupils develop self-awareness, resilience, healthy relationships and the skills to make informed choices about their wellbeing. The Religious Education curriculum allows them to deepen their understanding of diverse beliefs and worldviews and cultivate respect, empathy and open-mindedness towards others. Alongside this, our focus on SMSC (Spiritual, Moral, Social and Cultural development) and British Values ensures that pupils explore fundamental principles such as democracy, the rule of law, individual liberty, mutual respect and tolerance. Through assemblies, enrichment activities and school-wide initiatives – children celebrate diversity, learn the importance of equality and inclusion and cultivate empathy and compassion. These experiences equip pupils to contribute positively to society, develop strong social and emotional skills and grow as responsible, well-rounded individuals.
Wellbeing and personal growth are at the heart of school life. We support pupils’ emotional resilience, self-confidence and growth mindset while promoting physical and mental health, online and offline safety and age-appropriate learning about healthy relationships. By providing guidance and opportunities tailored to each stage of their education, North Ealing ensures that every child feels valued, supported and prepared to flourish academically, socially and personally in an ever-changing world.
Zone of Regulation
At North Ealing, we encourage children to talk about their emotions and feelings. To make this more manageable, we use a system that categorizes feelings, levels of alertness, and energy into four coloured zones: Blue, Green, Yellow, and Red.
We invite parents and carers to use the resources below at home to support your child in continuing to express their emotions. These resources include helpful tips for each zone, along with a breathing exercise to promote self-regulation and well-being.
Children’s Well-Being Charter
Our School Council has developed a Children’s Well-being Charter for all pupils at NEPS. This charter outlines the measures in place to support the well-being and mental health of every child.
It details the commitment of NEPS staff to fostering a supportive environment, as well as the resources and opportunities available to pupils to ensure their mental health and well-being are prioritized.
Staff Well Being Charter
At NEPS, we recognise the importance of supporting the mental health and well-being of our staff. This year, we have developed our own Staff Well-being Charter, incorporating the views and suggestions of our team to create a positive and supportive work environment.
Our charter outlines the measures in place to ensure that all staff feel valued, supported, and empowered in the workplace.

Art and Design Curriculum
Art and Design Curriculum
Every child is an artist.
Our North Ealing Primary School we value the importance of Art and Design in the curriculum to stimulate creativity, imagination and individuality.
We aim to inspire, challenge and provide our children with a clear purpose for creating their artwork and provide them with a good understanding of how art reflects and shapes our history and contributes to the culture, creativity and wealth of our nation.
Implementation
In the Early Years Foundation Stage (EYFS), Expressive Arts and Design includes two strands: Creating with Materials, where children explore materials to express ideas, and Being Imaginative and Expressive, where they develop imagination through role play, music and performance. Art in Nursery is guided by Development Matters, often linked to celebrations and events, while Reception follows the EYFS statutory framework and aligns with the Kapow scheme to ensure progression and a smooth transition into Year 1.
We follow the ‘Kapow Primary’ scheme of work, in Years 1-6, to shape our curriculum, adapting it to meet the needs of our pupils. This is structured around four key strands:
● Drawing● Painting and Mixed Media● Sculpture and 3D● Craft and Design.
Within these areas, pupils develop skills in generating ideas, using sketchbooks, mastering making skills (including formal elements), acquiring knowledge of the arts, and engaging in evaluation and analysis.
Key skills are revisited regularly with increasing complexity through a spiral curriculum model, allowing pupils to consolidate and build upon their prior learning.
Children receive either a weekly art lesson or a 2.5-day block of lessons.
Our school’s locality easily allows for planned opportunities for learning outside the classroom, as well as the involvement of adults with specialist skills from the local and wider community.
Impact
The structure of the art curriculum ensures that children are able to develop their knowledge and understanding of the work of artists, craftspeople and designers from a range of times and cultures and apply this knowledge to their own work.
Children use sketchbooks to record, explore, and store visual information, notes, and materials. They also use them to work out ideas, plans, and designs, as well as to track the development of their work. The sketchbook serves as a tool for reflecting on and reviewing progress, and as a record of their learning and achievements, helping them to further develop their ideas, skills, and understanding.
Displays reflect the children’s sense of pride in their artwork and this is also demonstrated by creative outcomes across the wider curriculum. The Art curriculum at NEPS contributes to children’s personal development and is underpinned by our school Learning Values.
Art & Design Curriculum – For parents and students

● Planning and creativity: Pupils practise organising ideas, following multi-step processes, and experimenting with different media, supporting problem-solving and expressive skills.

pageCache.text:
Computing Curriculum
Computing Curriculum
Technology can become the ‘wings’ that will allow the educational world to fly farther and faster than ever before; if we will allow it.
Intent
At our school, we want every child to become a confident, creative and safe user of technology. Our Computing curriculum is designed to give pupils the knowledge and skills they need to understand how technology works, how to use it responsibly, and how to solve problems through logical thinking.
We follow the Teach Computing curriculum, which ensures a clear progression of knowledge and skills from EYFS to Year 6. Our intent is that all pupils:
● Develop a strong understanding of computer science, including algorithms and programming● Use a range of information technology tools to create, organise and present work● Become responsible, respectful and safe users of technology through high‑quality online safety teaching● Build resilience, creativity and problem‑solving skills that prepare them for a digital world
We aim to ensure Computing is inclusive, engaging and accessible for all learners.
Implementation
We deliver Computing through the Teach Computing scheme, which provides a carefully sequenced curriculum built around four key strands:
● Computer Science – understanding algorithms, programming, debugging and logical reasoning● Information Technology – using software to create digital content such as text, images, audio and data● Digital Literacy – using technology safely, respectfully and responsibly● Online Safety – taught regularly and progressively across the school
EYFSChildren explore technology through play, using tablets, cameras and simple software. They learn to follow instructions, use age‑appropriate apps and understand basic online safety rules.
Key Stage 1Pupils begin to understand what algorithms are, create simple programs and learn how to debug them. They use digital tools to create and organise content and learn how to stay safe online.
Key Stage 2Pupils build on their programming knowledge using more complex sequences, variables and events. They use a wide range of software for different purposes, understand networks and the internet, and develop a deeper understanding of online safety and digital responsibility.
Teaching Approach● Lessons include modelling, guided practice and independent tasks● Vocabulary is explicitly taught and revisited● Retrieval practice helps pupils remember key concepts● Devices are used purposefully and safely● SEND pupils are supported through scaffolding, visuals and adapted tools
Impact
By the time pupils leave Year 6, they will:
● Be confident, competent and creative users of technology● Understand how computers and programs work● Be able to design, write and debug their own programs● Use a range of digital tools to create high‑quality content● Know how to stay safe online and make responsible choices● Talk confidently about their learning using correct vocabulary● Show clear progression in their knowledge and skills across the school
We measure impact through:● Pupil voice● Work samples and digital portfolios● Teacher assessment against learning objectives● Observations of practical skills● Monitoring of online safety understanding
Our Computing curriculum ensures pupils are well‑prepared for the digital world and ready for the next stage of their education.

pageCache.text:
English Curriculum
English Curriculum
English has a pre-eminent place in education and in society. A high-quality education in English will teach pupils to speak and write fluently so that they can communicate their ideas and emotions to others and through their reading and listening, others can communicate with them.
Through reading in particular, pupils have a chance to develop culturally, emotionally, intellectually, socially and spiritually.
(National Curriculum, September 2013)
At North Ealing Primary School, our aim is to ensure every child is encouraged and supported to become a keen and fluent reader, an articulate speaker and a confident writer. Thus preparing them for the next stage in their learning journey.
The English curriculum comprises many interwoven aspects: speaking and listening, reading fluency and comprehension, vocabulary acquisition, spelling, handwriting, an understanding of grammar and articulating ideas in order to structure them in writing.
Spellings
Spelling and handwriting are the two key transcription skills which the children need to master in order to become confident and fluent writers. They need to be able to spell quickly and accurately through knowing the relationship between sounds and letters (phonics) and understanding the spelling structure of words.
How spelling is taught at North Ealing Primary School
At North Ealing Primary School, we use the Read Write Inc Phonic programme to teach children in the Early Years and Year 1 how to read and spell.
• Children learn phoneme/sound correspondence and blend sounds together to read and spell green words – phonetically decodable words.• Children also learn how to spell Red words – those which have a non-decodable element and therefore are best learned by sight and memory.
For children in Years 2 to 6, we use the Read Write Inc Spelling programme. This enables us to meet the spelling expectations of the National Curriculum 2014 (Appendix 1: Spelling) and provides consistency and progression in the teaching of spelling.
Read Write Inc Spelling is an interactive programme which teaches spellings in a fun and engaging way. It helps children to learn spellings with common patterns and uses rules in order to help them recall spellings as well as teaching exceptions to these rules.
The teaching naturally follows on from the Read Write Inc phonics programme taught as soon as the children enter North Ealing Primary School. Therefore the children are already proficient at using dots (for individual sounds) and dashes (for Special Friends/digraphs and trigraphs) and prefixes and suffixes can be added to root words to help them to spell with greater accuracy, understanding and confidence. Weekly spelling lists are taken home for children to practise and consolidate their spelling.
By the end of year 6:
At North Ealing Primary School, our aim is that children should be able to:
• Understand and apply the spelling rules taught throughout KS1 and KS2.• Have an understanding that some words do not follow these rules and just need to be learnt. (Those listed in the National Curriculum English Appendix 1.) • Children are given regular opportunities to use a dictionary, both to check the spelling of some words and the meaning.
English Appendix – Spellings – Click here
How to support your child with their spelling at home
Regular practice of weekly spellings has been shown to help embed spelling patterns as well as individual exception words. Support your child with learning their weekly spelling list by reading out each word for them to write down and helping them with any words they are finding particularly tricky., for example by using a mnemonic rhyme.
Speaking & Listening
Spoken language underpins the development of reading and writing and at North Ealing, we believe that oracy is a powerful tool for learning. By teaching pupils to become more effective speakers and listeners we empower them to better understand themselves, each other and the world around them. Through a high quality oracy education, developed in collaboration with Voice 21 a national oracy education charity, students learn through talk and to talk.
How oracy is taught at North Ealing Primary School
Oracy is taught across the curriculum, with the children being given well planned opportunities to develop their speaking and listening skills both with their talk partners and in larger groups. They are encouraged to build on, respectfully challenge, clarify and probe others’ ideas; summarise discussions; debate and present. By embedding these practices throughout their learning, children learn the skills needed to talk effectively as well as developing and deepening their subject knowledge and understanding.
Spoken language underpins the development of reading and writing and at North Ealing, we believe that oracy is a powerful tool for learning. By teaching pupils to become more effective speakers and listeners we empower them to better understand themselves, each other and the world around them. Through a high quality oracy education, developed in collaboration with Voice 21 a national oracy education charity, students learn through talk and to talk.
By the end of year 6:
By the end of year 6, we aim for every child at North Ealing Primary School to:
• Have the confidence and skills to listen and speak effectively in a range of situations.• Be able to share their ideas in class, lead discussions and present in assemblies.• Be active listeners, responding thoughtfully and respectfully to others.• Ask insightful questions which deepen their understanding and encourage meaningful discussion.
Link to the oracy section on the website: Click here.
Reading
Reading is a key life skill and fundamental to all aspects of education. Extensive research indicates that children who read for pleasure are more likely to develop a broader and richer vocabulary, increase their general knowledge and perform well across all subjects.
At North Ealing Primary School, we help to nurture a love of reading by encouraging and supporting children to read every day and through carefully selected high quality texts which are at the heart of our curriculum.
Our aim is to equip each reader with the tools to tackle unfamiliar vocabulary and diverse materials. We want our children to recommend books to their peers and enjoy reading a wide range of genres, including non-fiction. We encourage children to participate in book talk, including evaluating an author’s use of language and how this can affect the reader. We encourage our pupils to see themselves as discerning readers and to be confident in discussing not only whether they enjoy a text but also the extent to which they agree with it.
How reading is taught at North Ealing Primary School
Reading consists of two key elements: word recognition and language comprehension. Both these are taught explicitly and discretely across all key stages.
In the Early Years and KS1, pupils learn to read accurately and fluently through daily phonics lessons following our Read Write Inc phonics scheme. Additional phonics interventions take place for those children identified as needing some extra support.
Link to phonics on the website: Click here.
In addition, all children follow our Rising Stars reading scheme, reading regularly to adults at school as well as at home.
Teachers share stories, rhymes and information texts with children on a daily basis, developing their interest and pleasure in reading. In Year 2 whole class comprehension lessons deepen children’s ability to explore and understand a range of genres.
In years 2-6, whole class fluency lessons develop children’s vocabulary, prosody and automaticity skills in order that comprehension of the text can take place. Children also practice discussing and independently answering a range of comprehension questions.
Children who are not yet ‘free readers’ continue to work through our school reading scheme- levelled books which match the children’s current reading age.
High quality texts are at the heart of our English lessons, giving the children regular opportunities to listen to texts being read out loud and to read out loud themselves both individually and with whole class choral reading. Teachers model expressive, fluent reading and build in regular opportunities to discuss new and adventurous vocabulary. Text analysis also forms part of every English unit, with time built into units for children to discuss what their thoughts are towards the text. This is before they move on to applying the skills of analysis, retrieval, prediction and inference to what they have read.
Pupils’ comprehension skills are formally assessed termly and any gaps in learning are addressed either through whole class teaching or individual and small group booster classes.
Reading for pleasure is also modelled and encouraged through regular story time, quiet reading time and time being given for children to read and choose their own books from their class library or our school library.
We also have a number of reading enrichment activities across the year, including visits by children’s authors (including poets), World Book Day events and reading challenges.
Link to our core text overview for Yr 1-6: Click here.
By the end of year 6:
At the end of year 6, our aim is for all children to:
• Leave as confident, enthusiastic readers who read for pleasure as well as to boost their learning across all subjects.• Have a secure understanding of the different reading skills which are formally assessed at the end of KS2 and be able to apply them confidently to a wide range of genres (including non-fiction and poetry).• Able to discuss and evaluate an increasingly wide range of fiction and non-fiction texts and to give their opinion on these.
How to support your child with their reading at home
Reading daily to young children helps build key language and social skills. Once children start bringing home school books (RWI books, books from our Rising Stars scheme and library books), share these together and take the time to listen to your child read their book to you every day.

Writing
Learning to write is one of the hardest challenges pupils face at school but it is vitally important: learning to speak, read and write well are crucial for children and young people’s success in education, life and work. Pupils who find it difficult to express their ideas in writing are likely to struggle across the curriculum, not just in English. (The writing framework July 2025) Alongside spelling and handwriting, becoming a fluent writer depends on articulating and structuring ideas (the compositional skills) in order that children are able to communicate their thoughts and ideas to a range of different audiences.
How writing is taught at North Ealing Primary School
From EYFS, children at North Ealing Primary School are taught a highly effective and engaging writing curriculum which uses high quality core texts as models for writing. These texts form the basis of our English lessons and are often linked to other topics being studied (for example in history or science).
Early writers are given regular opportunities to practise the transcription skills of spelling and handwriting including writing sentences which are dictated to them. Alongside this, high quality oracy opportunities which include role play, storytelling and rhyme stimulate ideas for shared writing.
Older children also have regular, high quality oracy opportunities to stimulate ideas for writing including writing for real purposes and genuine audiences. The writing sequence involves the children deconstructing and analysing high quality model texts which their teachers have prepared as well as opportunities for shared writing alongside the teacher. Grammar is introduced and taught in a meaningful way as part of this process. Teachers also model and teach the children how to edit, evaluate and improve their written work both independently and with a writing partner.
By the end of year 6:
By the end of their primary school journey, pupils should be able to:
• Write effectively for a range of purposes and audiences, selecting language that shows good awareness of the reader.• Describe settings, characters and atmosphere in narrative writing.• Integrate dialogue in narratives to convey character and advance the action.• Appropriately select vocabulary and grammatical structures that reflect what the writing requires.• Use a range of devices to build cohesion within and across paragraphs (e.g. conjunctions, adverbials of time and place, pronouns, synonyms).• Use verb tenses consistently and correctly throughout their writing.• Use the range of punctuation taught at key stage 2 mostly correctly (e.g. inverted commas and other punctuation to indicate direct speech; some use of colons and semi-colons and dashes; bullet points and hyphens).• Spell correctly most words from the year 5 / year 6 spelling list and use a dictionary to check the spelling of uncommon or more ambitious vocabulary.• Maintain legibility in joined handwriting when writing at speed.
How to support your child with their handwriting at home:
In addition to supporting your child when practising their weekly spelling words, provide a range of writing opportunities, e.g. writing letters, shopping lists, party invitations etc. Encourage your child to speak in full sentences using correct Standard English. When reading with and to your child, explicitly point out and discuss new vocabulary and encourage them to use it.
Handwriting
At North Ealing Primary School, we ensure that high standards of handwriting and presentation are established from EYFS. Geography Curriculum
Geography Curriculum
‘What is our knowledge worth if we know nothing about the world that sustains us, nothing about natural systems and climate, nothing about countries and cultures?’
Jonathon Porritt, Forum of the Future
At North Ealing Primary School (NEPS), geography is a vital part of our curriculum, enabling pupils to understand the world they live in and their role within it. In our diverse school community, we recognise the importance of developing pupils’ awareness of different cultures, environments and global issues, fostering respect, curiosity and a sense of responsibility as global citizens.
In the Early Years Foundation Stage (EYFS), learning follows the Development Matters guidance, supporting children to develop an early understanding of the world through the areas of Past and Present, People, Culture and Communities and The Natural World. Children begin to explore their environment, make sense of their surroundings and develop curiosity about the world around them.
In Key Stages 1 and 2, our geography curriculum builds on these foundations, developing pupils’ knowledge and understanding of the world and their place within it. We aim to inspire a lifelong curiosity and fascination about the world and its people, while promoting respect for diverse places, cultures and environments. Pupils develop an understanding of both physical and human geography, as well as the importance of environmental sustainability.
Our curriculum is carefully sequenced to ensure that knowledge and skills are progressive and transferable. At the start of each topic, pupils reflect on prior learning, share what they already know and generate questions to guide their enquiry. Cross-curricular links are planned for and our local area is used extensively to provide meaningful, real-life learning experiences that support deeper understanding and “sticky” knowledge.
Geographical learning is underpinned by our Curriculum Principles, enabling pupils to make connections across subjects and over time. Outcomes are assessed through pupils’ ability to ask perceptive questions, think critically and apply key geographical skills, alongside the work recorded work in books.
Through this approach, we equip pupils with the knowledge, skills and awareness they need to understand the world and become responsible, informed and environmentally conscious global citizens.
Unicef Rights – Article 29
Education must develop every child’s personality, talents and abilities to the full. It must encourage the child’s respect for human rights, as well as respect for their parents, their own and other cultures, and the environment.

History Curriculum
History Curriculum
‘A people without knowledge of their past history, origin and culture is like a tree without roots.’
History has always been held in high regard at North Ealing Primary School (NEPS), with the school’s own rich history and its place within the local community providing a celebrated and inspiring context for learning. Our curriculum makes full use of the immediate and wider local area, enabling children to develop a deep understanding of the history of their locality and its significance over time.
In the Early Years Foundation Stage (EYFS), learning follows the Development Matters guidance, supporting children to develop an early understanding of the world through the areas of Past and Present, People, Culture and Communities and The Natural World.
In Key Stages 1 and 2, we deliver an enquiring and coherent history curriculum which enables all children to develop a secure knowledge and understanding of Britain’s past and that of the wider world. Pupils are encouraged to ask perceptive questions, think critically, weigh evidence and develop perspective and judgement. Through this, they begin to understand the complexity of people’s lives, the process of change, the diversity of societies and relationships between different groups.
Our curriculum is carefully sequenced, with key knowledge and skills identified for each topic to ensure clear progression across year groups. By the end of Year 6, pupils develop a strong chronological understanding of British history from the Stone Age to the present day, alongside studies of world history, including ancient civilisations such as Greece and Egypt. Pupils are able to draw comparisons, make connections between time periods and relate historical learning to their own lives, with a strong emphasis on community and local context.
Historical learning is underpinned by our Curriculum Principles, promoting enquiry, oracy and critical thinking. Outcomes in history are based on agreed success criteria, pupils’ ability to ask perceptive questions and think critically, the quality of recorded work in books and the development and application of key historical skills.
Through this approach, we aim to develop curious, reflective learners who understand the past and are equipped to make sense of the present and future.

Mathematics Curriculum
Mathematics Curriculum
Mathematics is a tool for everyday life. It teaches children to make sense of the world around them through developing their ability to calculate, to reason and to solve problems. Our aim when teaching maths at North Ealing Primary school (NEPS) is to develop children’s confidence and attitude towards maths through a fun, inclusive and ambitious programme.
In EYFS we follow the ‘Development Matters in EYFS’ guidance. In KS1 and 2 we use Power Maths to deliver the National Curriculum through a whole-class mastery approach. There is a large focus on a deep understanding of number and the number generic equivalent for ventolin system. In maths lessons, children follow an enquiring approach to investigate, discuss and solve problems. Teachers consistently use the CPA (concrete, pictorial, abstract) approach for problem-solving to help children develop mastery in both written and mental methods across all the operations in an efficient and reliable way.
Children are given real-life problems so that their learning is both accessible and relatable; they can see the importance of using and applying maths in their everyday lives. Teachers challenge learners by asking them to explain their thinking and communicate mathematical methods and strategies, using mathematical language appropriately. Our lessons are lively and engaging and there are opportunities for children to work independently and collaboratively.
Regular and ongoing assessment informs teaching, as well as intervention, to support and enable the success of every child. We emphasise to the children that their understanding of what they are learning is of great importance, as well as their ability to recall facts and figures in preparation for the next stage in their learning.
What the children will achieve by the end of KS2:

Occupational Therapy Support
● Spatial reasoning and problem-solving: OT strategies support pupils in developing these skills through visual-perceptual activities and motor planning tasks.
● Attention and focus: Pupils use movement breaks and sensory tools to help maintain concentration during mathematical tasks.
● Sequencing and memory: Structured activities, such as step-by-step problem-solving tasks or visual timelines, help pupils organise and retain mathematical procedures.
● Fine motor skills for maths tasks: Manipulating objects, using rulers, counters, or shapes supports hand-eye coordination and practical engagement with mathematical concepts.

PSHE Curriculum
Dear Parents and Carers,
As we approach the second half of the summer term, children will be focusing on Relationships and Health Education as part of their PSHE lessons. This forms part of our Health Education programme and is in line with the London Borough of Ealing’s scheme of work for Personal, Social, Health and Economic (PSHE) Education.
Our lessons are carefully planned to be age-appropriate, sensitive and engaging, providing children with opportunities for thoughtful discussion and learning. We will be using resources from the Ealing Local Authority PSHE scheme of work, alongside content from the National Curriculum for Science (2014).
In Reception and Key Stage 1, children will explore friendships, families, personal hygiene, feelings, trusted adults and ways to keep themselves safe in an age-appropriate and sensitive manner. From Key Stage 2 onwards, children will explore the statutory health topic of developing bodies, learning about the physical and emotional changes that occur as they grow and prepare for the next stage of life. They will also learn about healthy relationships, family life, and the role of trusted adults and professionals in helping to keep them safe.
Please note that Relationships Education is a statutory part of the PSHE curriculum in all primary schools. For Year 6 pupils, there is one additional non-statutory lesson on conception and pregnancy. This lesson builds upon children’s understanding of puberty and the reproductive system by explaining the scientific process of reproduction in an age-appropriate way. Parents and carers have the right to withdraw their child from this specific lesson. However, we encourage families to speak with the school and the PSHE Lead before making this decision.
Our aim is to ensure that all children grow up happy, healthy and safe. This aspect of the curriculum is an important part of helping children develop the knowledge and skills needed to make informed and safe choices throughout their lives. The curriculum follows a spiral approach, meaning children revisit and build upon key concepts gradually in ways that are appropriate for their age and stage of development.
If you would like further information, we will be holding a parent workshop to discuss the upcoming curriculum content in more detail.
Parent Workshop• Thursday 11th June• 9:00 am• New Hall
During the workshop, we will discuss the statutory Relationships and Health Education curriculum, as well as the Year 6 non-statutory sex education lesson and the content covered within it. A copy of the presentation will also be made available on the school website following the workshop.
To support parents and carers in understanding the curriculum content, please see the Summer Term RSE learning questions for each year group below please also find attached the Summer Term RSE learning objectives to this email for your reference.
If you have any questions or concerns after reading the information or attending the workshop, please do not hesitate to speak to me or your child’s class teacher.
Kind regards,Mrs Tranter

Personal, Social, Health and Economics (PSHE) Curriculum
At North Ealing Primary School (NEPS) our Personal, Social, Health and Economic (PSHE) curriculum aims to enable pupils to become healthy, independent and responsible members of society. We strive to deliver PSHE lessons which are accessible to all and ensure that each of our pupils will know more, remember more and understand more about how to play a positive and successful role within our society, both as a child and as an adult in the future.
Our PSHE provision is closely linked to our school values and ethos, promoting resilience, responsibility and respect for others. Through engaging, inclusive and reflective learning experiences, we develop pupils’ confidence and self-esteem, preparing them to navigate an ever-changing world with empathy, integrity and ambition.
PSHE is central to our pastoral care and whole-school approach. As a UNICEF Gold Rights Respecting School, children learn about their rights and the rights of others, supporting our commitment to wellbeing, inclusion, equality and high aspirations for every child.
Our PSHE scheme of work incorporates British Values and promotes respect for the Protected Characteristics set out in the Equality Act 2010. We follow the Ealing PSHE Scheme of Work, which meets the statutory requirements for Relationships Education, RSE and Health Education – see video link below and ( link to RHE policy) , ensuring pupils feel safe, valued and prepared for life in modern Britain.
Promoting British Values and SMSC through PSHE
PSHE at North Ealing Primary School plays a central role in promoting pupils’ Spiritual, Moral, Social and Cultural (SMSC) development and British Values, supporting pupils to become confident, respectful and responsible members of modern British society.
Through PSHE, pupils develop an age-appropriate understanding of the fundamental British Values of democracy, the rule of law, individual liberty, and mutual respect and tolerance of those with different faiths and beliefs. These values are explored through discussion, reflection, pupil voice and real-life contexts, enabling pupils to understand their rights and responsibilities within school and wider society. Each half term, carefully chosen texts are used to support learning in PSHE, explicitly linking to British Values, SMSC themes and the Protected Characteristics.
SMSC underpins all aspects of PSHE and wider school life (see SMSC policy). While not taught as a discrete subject, it is embedded through the PSHE curriculum and wider learning, providing regular opportunities for pupils to reflect, develop moral reasoning and consider the impact of their choices.
A structured programme of assemblies reinforces key PSHE themes and draws on a wide range of cultural, social and global contexts. Class floor books capture pupils’ reflections and learning across PSHE and the wider curriculum, supporting progression and deeper understanding over time.
UNICEF Rights – Article 13
You have the right to find out things and share what you think with others, by talking, drawing, writing or in any other way unless it harms or offends other people.
